docker_prune_desc: Docker accumulates old build layers, dangling images, and stopped containers. This action cleans everything not in active use without affecting running containers.
logs_desc: Files in /var/log and Linux journals can grow indefinitely. Compressed files (.gz, .log.1) are safe to delete.
cache_desc: The package manager retains downloaded .deb files in /var/cache/apt/archives.
trash_desc: Items deleted via File Manager stay in the safe trash. Empty to permanently reclaim physical storage.
safety_intro: Orbit blocks the deletion of critical essential directories. Below is the detailed list of what should NEVER be deleted manually via terminal or scripts to prevent irreversible host corruption.
boot_desc: Contains Linux kernels, Initramfs and Grub. If deleted, the server will not boot.
docker_overlay_desc: Docker internal storage driver layers. Never use rm -rf directly here. Always use docker system prune.
etc_desc: Global operating system configurations (fstab, passwd, network, etc.).
lib_desc: Shared libraries (.so) required by virtually all system binaries.
proc_desc: Virtual filesystems generated in RAM by the kernel. They do not consume actual disk space.
tmp_desc: Temporary session and process files. Can be cleaned safely.
cache_home_desc: Browser and CLI tool caches. Can be deleted without permanent data loss.
var_lib_desc: Contains active database data (Postgres, MySQL, Redis) and application volumes.
config_home_desc: User preferences and application configuration keys.
safety_critical_desc: DO NOT DELETE manually. Essential for the operation of the kernel and operating system.
safety_warning_desc: May contain databases, container volumes, or active application settings.
safety_safe_desc: Temporary cache, rotated logs, or trash that can be freed without affecting the system.
safety_user_data_desc: User or application files and folders.
safety_user_desc: User or application files and folders.
